In [[geometry]], the '''rhombicosidodecahedron''' is an [[Archimedean solid]], one of thirteen [[Convex polyhedron|convex]] [[Isogonal figure|isogonal]] nonprismatic solids constructed of two or more types of [[regular polygon]] [[Face (geometry)|face]]s.

It has a total of 62 faces: 20 regular [[triangular]] faces, 30 [[square (geometry)|square]] faces, 12 regular [[pentagon]]al faces, with 60 [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]], and 120 [[edge (geometry)|edges]].
[[File:Rhombicosidodecahedron.stl|thumb|3D model of a rhombicosidodecahedron]]

==Names==
{{multiple image
| align = left
| total_width = 350

| image1 = Nonuniform rhombicosidodecahedron as rectified rhombic triacontahedron max.png
| image2 = Rhombicosidodecahedron in rhombic triacontahedron max.png
| image3 = Nonuniform rhombicosidodecahedron as core of dual compound max.png

[[Johannes Kepler]] in ''[[Harmonices Mundi]]'' (1618) named this polyhedron a ''rhombicosidodecahedron'', being short for ''truncated icosidodecahedral rhombus'', with ''icosidodecahedral rhombus'' being his name for a [[rhombic triacontahedron]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Ioannis Keppler [''i.e.'', [[Johannes Kepler]]]|chapter=Liber II. De Congruentia Figurarum Harmonicarum. XXVIII. Propositio.|trans-chapter=Book II. On the Congruence of Harmonic Figures. Proposition XXVIII.|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/ioanniskepplerih00kepl/page/n87/mode/1up|title=[[Harmonices Mundi|Harmonices Mundi Libri V]]|trans-title=The Harmony of the World in Five Books|location=Linz, Austria|publisher=Sumptibus Godofredi Tampachii bibl. Francof. excudebat Ioannes Plancus [published by Gottfried Tambach [...] printed by Johann Planck]|year=1619|page=64|oclc=863358134|quote=Unus igitur Trigonicus cum duobus Tetragonicis & uno Pentagonico, minus efficiunt 4 rectis, & congruunt 20 Trigonicum 30 Tetragonis & 12 Pentagonis, in unum Hexacontadyhedron, quod appello Rhombicoſidodecaëdron, ſeu ſectum Rhombum Icoſidododecaëdricum.}}</ref><ref>''Harmonies Of The World'' by Johannes Kepler, Translated into English with an introduction and notes by ''E. J. Aiton'', ''A. M. Duncan'', ''[[Judith V. Field|J. V. Field]]'', 1997, {{isbn|0-87169-209-0}} (page 123)</ref> There are different truncations of a [[rhombic triacontahedron]] into a [[topology|topological]] rhombicosidodecahedron: Prominently its [[rectification (geometry)|rectification]] (left), the one that creates the uniform solid (center), and the rectification of the dual [[icosidodecahedron]] (right), which is the core of the [[dual compound]].

==Dimensions==
For a rhombicosidodecahedron with edge length ''a'', its surface area and volume are:

:<math>\begin{align} A &= \left(30+5\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{25+10\sqrt{5}}\right)a^2 &&\approx 59.305\,982\,844\,9 a^2 \\ V &=\frac{60+29\sqrt{5}}{3}a^3 &&\approx 41.615\,323\,782\,5 a^3 \end{align}</math>

==Geometric relations==
Cantellating either a [[regular dodecahedron]] or [[regular icosahedron]] produces a rhombicosidodecahedron.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-10-08 |title=Small rhombicosidodecahedron |url=https://polytope.miraheze.org/wiki/Small_rhombicosidodecahedron |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=Polytope Wiki |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:P4-A11-P5.gif|thumb|Cantellation of either a regular dodecahedron or a regular icosahedron creates a rhombicosidodecahedron.]]
[[Expansion (geometry)|Expanding]] an [[icosidodecahedron]] by moving the faces away from the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] the right amount, rotating each face so that each triangle vertex continues to touch a pentagon vertex, without changing the size of the faces, and patching the square holes in the result, yields a rhombicosidodecahedron. Therefore, it has the same number of triangles as an [[icosahedron]] and the same number of pentagons as a [[dodecahedron]], with a square for each edge of either.

Alternatively, [[Expansion (geometry)|expanding]] each of five cubes by moving the faces away from the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] the right amount and rotating each of the five 72° around so they are equidistant from each other, without changing the orientation or size of the faces, and patching the pentagonal and triangular holes in the result, yields a rhombicosidodecahedron. Therefore, it has the same number of squares as five cubes.

Two clusters of faces of the [[bilunabirotunda]], the ''lunes'' (each ''lune'' featuring two triangles adjacent to opposite sides of one square), can be aligned with a congruent patch of faces on the rhombicosidodecahedron. If two bilunabirotundae are aligned this way on opposite sides of the rhombicosidodecahedron, then a cube can be put between the bilunabirotundae at the very center of the rhombicosidodecahedron.

The rhombicosidodecahedron shares the vertex arrangement with the [[small stellated truncated dodecahedron]], and with the uniform compounds of six or twelve [[pentagrammic prism]]s.

The [[Zometool]] kits for making [[geodesic dome]]s and other [[Polyhedron|polyhedra]] use slotted balls as connectors. The balls are "expanded" rhombicosidodecahedra, with the squares replaced by rectangles. The expansion is chosen so that the resulting rectangles are [[golden rectangle]]s.

Twelve of the 92 [[Johnson solid]]s are derived from the rhombicosidodecahedron, four of them by rotation of one or more [[pentagonal cupola]]e: the [[gyrate rhombicosidodecahedron|gyrate]], [[parabigyrate rhombicosidodecahedron|parabigyrate]], [[metabigyrate rhombicosidodecahedron|metabigyrate]], and [[trigyrate rhombicosidodecahedron]]. Eight more can be constructed by removing up to three cupolae, sometimes also rotating one or more of the other cupolae.

==Cartesian coordinates==
[[Cartesian coordinates]] for the vertices of a rhombicosidodecahedron with an edge length of 2 centered at the origin are all [[even permutation]]s of:<ref>{{mathworld |title=Icosahedral group |urlname=IcosahedralGroup}}</ref>
:(±1, ±1, ±''φ''<sup>3</sup>),
:(±''φ''<sup>2</sup>, ±''φ'', ±2''φ''),
:(±(2+''φ''), 0, ±''φ''<sup>2</sup>),
where ''φ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{sfrac|1 + {{sqrt|5}}|2}} is the [[golden ratio]]. Therefore, the [[circumradius]] of this rhombicosidodecahedron is the common distance of these points from the origin, namely {{sqrt|''φ''<sup>6</sup>+2}} = {{sqrt|''8φ+7''}} for edge length 2. For unit edge length, R must be halved, giving 
:''R'' = {{sfrac|{{sqrt|8''φ''+7}}|2}} = {{sfrac|{{sqrt|11+4{{sqrt|5}}}}|2}} &asymp; 2.233.

== Orthogonal projections ==
The ''rhombicosidodecahedron'' has six special [[orthogonal projection]]s, centered, on a vertex, on two types of edges, and three types of faces: triangles, squares, and pentagons. The last two correspond to the A<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> [[Coxeter plane]]s.

==Spherical tiling==
The rhombicosidodecahedron can also be represented as a [[spherical tiling]], and projected onto the plane via a [[stereographic projection]]. This projection is [[Conformal map|conformal]], preserving angles but not areas or lengths. Straight lines on the sphere are projected as circular arcs on the plane.

=== Symmetry mutations ===
This polyhedron is topologically related as a part of a sequence of [[Cantellation (geometry)|cantellated]] polyhedra with vertex figure (3.4.n.4), which continues as tilings of the [[Hyperbolic space|hyperbolic plane]]. These [[vertex-transitive]] figures have (*n32) reflectional [[Orbifold notation|symmetry]].

{{Expanded small table}}

===Vertex arrangement===
The rhombicosidodecahedron shares its [[vertex arrangement]] with three [[nonconvex uniform polyhedra]]: the [[small stellated truncated dodecahedron]], the [[small dodecicosidodecahedron]] (having the triangular and pentagonal faces in common), and the [[small rhombidodecahedron]] (having the square faces in common).

It also shares its vertex arrangement with the [[Polyhedron compound#Uniform compounds|uniform compounds]] of [[compound of six pentagrammic prisms|six]] or [[compound of twelve pentagrammic prisms|twelve pentagrammic prisms]].

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], a '''rhombicosidodecahedral graph''' is the [[1-skeleton|graph of vertices and edges]] of the rhombicosidodecahedron, one of the [[Archimedean solid]]s. It has 60 [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and 120 edges, and is a [[quartic graph]] [[Archimedean graph]].<ref>{{citation|last1=Read|first1=R. C.|last2=Wilson|first2=R. J.|author-link2=Robin Wilson (mathematician)|title=An Atlas of Graphs|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year= 1998|page=269}}</ref>
